title: On the Existence of an Extremal Function for the Delsarte Extremal Problem

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract says that an extremal function exists "when Ω is closed." This is false without the additional assumption that Ω is a neighbourhood of 0. The paper itself later states that the admissible class is empty when 0 is not in int Ω. For example, in G=R, Ω={0} is closed and has finite Haar measure, but no continuous positive-definite f with f(0)=1 can have supp f_+ contained in {0}, since continuity makes f positive in a neighbourhood of 0. The actual main theorem requires a "closed neighbourhood of 0," so the abstract materially overstates the result.

The proof states: "both \(\mathcal{G}_G(\Omega)\) and \(\mathcal{G}_H(\Omega)\) are empty. Therefore, both sides of (1) are equal to 0." But \(\mathcal D_G(\Omega)\) was defined as a supremum over \(\mathcal G_G(\Omega)\), and the supremum of an empty set is not 0 under the usual extended-real convention; it is −∞. No special convention defining the Delsarte constant of an empty class to be 0 is stated. Thus the asserted value 0, and this part of the proof, are unjustified as written.

The proof repeatedly writes integrals with respect to \(d\lambda_G(\Omega)\), e.g. "\(\int_G f(g)\,d\lambda_G(\Omega) \geq D_G(\Omega)>0\)" and later "\(\int_G h(g)\,d\lambda_G(\Omega)\)." Here \(\lambda_G(\Omega)\) is a scalar, not a measure on G, so these expressions are undefined. They must be \(d\lambda_G(g)\). This occurs at the key step used to conclude that f is nonzero and to derive the contradiction after rescaling.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 9 proof, final sentence asserting uniform compact convergence
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof concludes: "As in Theorem 8, \((f_n)\) converges to f uniformly on the compact subsets of H, and hence \((\tilde f_n)\) converges to \(\tilde f\) uniformly on the compact subsets of G." However, neither an extremal sequence \((f_n)\) in H nor its trivial extensions \((\tilde f_n)\) is introduced anywhere in the proof of Theorem 9. The existence part proves only an extremizer \(f\). Consequently the claimed approximation part of Theorem 9 is not actually proved. A corrected proof must explicitly take the approximating extremal sequence supplied by Theorem 8 on H, extend it by zero, and verify uniform convergence on arbitrary compact subsets of G.
